newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Annan hopes US will pay $1 billion in two years.
newsitem.headline: Annan hopes US will pay $1 billion in two years.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said on Thursday that he hoped the one billion dollars in U.S. arrears to the world body would be paid up over two years.
Annan also vowed to install a programme for U.N. reform that would be "visible and quantifiable".
But the new U.N. chief reiterated that the U.S. Senate should not set "arbitrary" benchmarks for U.N. reform before arrears were paid.

Annan was making his first official visit to the U.N. European headquarters a week after holding talks in Washington with President Clinton as well as with Senator Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
The U.S. administration was committed to paying its dues to the United Nations, which now make up one quarter of the budget, according to Annan.
"I think that the money will come," he told a news conference in Geneva.
"And I also that we think we can demonstrate that we are serious about reform. We will put in place a reform that is visible, that is quantifiable.
Annan said he had told the Senate it would be difficult if arbitrary targets were set without any relation to U.N. plans.
"If they keep current on future assessments and come up with plans to pay their arrears -- and we keep up with the reform -- I think we will all be all right."

"I think the intention now is to ensure that the amounts due to the U.N. are included in the President's budget and that the sum will be appropriated and be paid over a period of two years or so as we move forward with the reform -- with a commitment to remain current on future assessments," he added.
"In other words, I would expect that in time they would clear the arrears but undertake to pay future assessments in full and on time," the U.N. chief said.
On Wednesday, the Clinton administration unveiled a plan to clear up its $1 billion debt, but ran into criticism from Helms.

Representative Bill Richardson, Clinton's nominee as U.N. ambassador, said the administration would seek funding to cover the arrears but would delay payment until the 1999 fiscal year, beginning on Oct. 1, 1998. Washington would then pay only on condition that the United Nations met U.S. reform goals.
Congress has held up U.S. dues amid charges of U.N. waste and inefficiency. Helms told Annan he would seek legislation setting reform "benchmarks" to be met before arrears were paid.
"I had to to go to the Hill because they hold the power of the purse. I had to clear up certain misunderstandings," Annan said on Thursday.

"I believe that most of the Senators found the discussions and the explanations useful. They are honourable gentlemen and I am sure at the end of the day they will do the right thing and pay," he added.
Reform would be carried out in all U.N. duty stations, according to Annan, former head of U.N. peacekeeping operations.
"The main objective of the reform is to create a United Naitons that is leaner, efficient and effective in terms of aiming for the right results and right objectives..." he said.
"The emphasis is not going to be just cuts. To cut and not settle the issue of the role of the organisation, what it should be doing, is really not reform."
Annan said he had held talks with all five regional groups of member states and had won their support for reform.
"So the member states want reform, the staff want reform. We would all want to see an effective organisation.

"So what the United Nations wants is also what the U.S. wants. Since there is an agreement on this then I think we should be able to move forward and I look forward to the U.S. also paying its arrears to us."
